messages.subject: ezPerm methods?
parts:
Dear Group,

I am using exPerm to do a 1 way anova with repeated measures. I have
not found documentation pointing to how this works.

I have a treatment and control. I have 50 subjects, each were
submitted to treatment and control and then a dependent variable
measured on each under both conditions (treatment and control).

I'm assuming that the permutation step "respects" the repeated
measures by swapping individuals between treatment and control but
being sure that each individual is in each. Here is a toy example
with a small set.

SUBJECT GROUP DEPVAR
1 Treat 0.1
2 Treat 0.2
3 Treat 0.3
1 Control 0.5
2 Control 0.6
3 Control 0.7


Then one permutation of the above would be


SUBJECT GROUP DEPVAR
1 Treat 0.5
2 Treat 0.2
3 Treat 0.3
1 Control 0.1
2 Control 0.6
3 Control 0.7


Notice that all I did was swap values for subject 1.

Is this at all close?

Thanks,
Seth

messages.author: cb25d91fd630a4e5
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] ezPerm methods?
parts:
The "one within variable" case of the permutation test is the
simplest. It is implemented by computing each subject's difference
score between the conditions, computing the mean difference score,
then doing the following many times:
1) randomly change the sign of each score with a probability of .5
2) recompute the mean and store it

The percentile of the true mean is then computed with respect to the
resulting distribution of simulated means.

messages.author: cb25d91fd630a4e5
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] Re: ezPerm methods?
parts:
In my previous description of what happens with a 2-level within
variable, I described the computation of difference scores and
randomization of their sign. While this is formally equivalent to what
ezPerm does, what ezPerm actually does is slightly more flexible in
that it can deal with 2+ level within variables as well. ezPerm first
computes an F-value for the effect of the within variable, then
repeats the following many times
1) within each person, randomly reassign the condition labels to each data point
2) compute a new anova on the newly labelled data, yielding an F-value
that you keep for later

The percentile of the true F-value is then computed with respect to
the resulting distribution of simulated F-values.
